nodes.name: Weight initialization variance problem
nodes.statement: The problem can be stated as follows: If the weights in a neural network are initialized using samples from a normal distribution, ${\cal{N}}(0,v^{2})$, how should $v^{2}$ be chosen to ensure that the variance of the outputs from the different layers are approximately the same?
nodes.statement_short: How to choose the variance $v^{2}$ of a normal weight initialization so that all layers' output variances stay approximately equal.

nodes.name: Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: The first systematic analysis of this problem was conducted by Glorot and Bengio \cite{glorot2010understanding} who showed that for a linear activation function, the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer. Although the paper makes several assumptions about the inputs to the model, it works extremely well in many cases and is widely used in the initialization of neural networks to date; this initialization scheme is commonly referred to as the {\it{Xavier initialization}}.
nodes.statement_short: For linear activations the optimal initialization variance is $v^{2}=1/N$ (the Xavier initialization).
conclusions: the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer

nodes.name: He initialization
nodes.statement: In an important follow up paper, He and colleagues \cite{he2015delving} argue that the {\it{Xavier initialization}} does not work well with the RELU activation function, and instead propose an initialization of $v^{2} = 2/N$ (commonly referred to as the {\it{He initialization}}).
nodes.statement_short: He et al. argue Xavier fails for RELU and propose $v^{2}=2/N$ instead.
conclusions: propose an initialization of $v^{2} = 2/N$

nodes.name: 30 layer network supporting the He initialization
nodes.statement: In support of their initialization, they provide an example of a 30 layer neural network which converges with the {\it{He initialization}}, but not under the {\it{Xavier initialization}}.

nodes.name: Why one initialization converges and the other does not
nodes.statement: To the best of my knowledge, the precise reason for the convergence of one method and the non-convergence of the other is not fully understood.
nodes.statement_short: The mechanism behind convergence under the He initialization and non-convergence under Xavier is unexplained.

nodes.name: Summary of contributions
nodes.statement: My main contributions in this paper are to (a) generalize the results of \cite{glorot2010understanding} to the case of non-linear activation functions and (b) to provide a continuum between the results of \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving}. For the class of activation functions differentiable at 0, I provide a general initialization strategy. For the class of activation functions that are not differentiable at 0, I focus on the Rectified Linear Unit (RELU) and provide a rigorous proof of the {\it{He initialization}}. I also provide theoretical insights into why the 30 layer neural network converges with the {\it{He initialization}} but not with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}. As a small bonus, I resolve an unanswered question posed in \cite{glorot2010understanding} regarding the distributions of activations under the hyperbolic tangent activation.
nodes.statement_short: Contributions: generalize Glorot-Bengio to non-linear activations, prove the He initialization, and explain the tanh saturation puzzle.

nodes.name: deep neural network with $M$ layers
nodes.statement: Consider a deep neural network with $M$ layers. The relationship between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer ($x_{m}$) and $m+1^{th}$ layer ($x_{m+1}$) are described by the recursions \be y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij} \enum{in1} \ee and \be x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{g}(y_{m}(i)). \enum{in2} \ee Here $p_{j} = {\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)$, ${\bf{W}}_{m}$ is a matrix of weights for the $m^{th}$ layer, $g$ is the non-linear activation function, and $N$ is the number of nodes in the hidden layers respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Feed-forward model: pre-activations $y_{m}(i)$ are weighted sums of the layer inputs and $x_{m+1}=g(y_{m})$.

nodes.name: Pre-activation recursion
nodes.statement: \be y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij} \enum{in1} \ee
nodes.statement_short: The pre-activation of a node is the weighted sum $\sum_{j} p_{ij}$ of that layer's inputs.

nodes.name: Activation recursion
nodes.statement: \be x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{g}(y_{m}(i)). \enum{in2} \ee

nodes.name: Weights are i.i.d. normal with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$
nodes.statement: The weights ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ are assumed to be independent identically distributed normal random variables with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$.

nodes.name: First layer inputs are i.i.d. with mean 0 and variance 1
nodes.statement: Consistent with the assumptions in \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving}, I assume that the inputs to the first layer are independent and identically distributed random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.

nodes.name: $r_{m}$ and $u_{m}^{2}$ (mean and variance of $y_{m}(i)$)
nodes.statement: For convenience, I use $r_{m}$ and $u_{m}^{2}$ to denote the mean and variance of $y_{m}(i)$ respectively.

nodes.name: Symmetry of the layer input moments
nodes.statement: Due to the symmetry in the problem, all inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer will have the same means and variances during the first forward pass (i.e., $E(x_{m}(i)) = \mu_m$ and $Var(x_{m}(i)) = s_{m}^{2}$ for all $i$); the covariances between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer need not be 0.
nodes.statement_short: All inputs to a layer share the same mean $\mu_m$ and variance $s_m^{2}$ on the first forward pass, though they may be correlated.
assumptions: Due to the symmetry in the problem
conclusions: all inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer will have the same means and variances during the first forward pass
the covariances between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer need not be 0

nodes.name: Variance preservation goal
nodes.statement: The goal is to find the value of $v^{2}$ which ensures that $s_{1}^{2} \approx s_{2}^{2} ...\approx s_{M}^{2} = 1$ during the first forward pass.
nodes.statement_short: Find $v^{2}$ making all layer variances $s_{1}^{2}\approx\dots\approx s_{M}^{2}=1$.

nodes.name: Independence of weights and layer inputs
nodes.statement: During the first iteration, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$
conclusions: $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$

nodes.name: Proof of independence of weights and layer inputs
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in \eref{in1} and \eref{in2}, $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer. Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$. Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$
nodes.statement_short: Direct argument: $x_{m}(k)$ is a function only of earlier layers' weights and the first-layer inputs, all independent of $W_{m}$.

nodes.name: Express $x_{m}(k)$ through the recursions
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in \eref{in1} and \eref{in2}, $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer.
nodes.statement_short: Unroll the recursions to write $x_m(k)$ as a function of earlier weights and the first-layer inputs.

nodes.name: Independence is preserved by non-linear functions
nodes.statement: Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities.
nodes.statement_short: Layer-$m$ weights stay independent of any function of the quantities they are independent of.

nodes.name: Conclude independence
nodes.statement: Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude that $W_m(i,j)$ is independent of $x_m(k)$ for all indices.

nodes.name: Extend independence to products
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$
nodes.statement_short: Extend the conclusion to the product $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$.

nodes.name: Derivation of the pre-activation variance
nodes.statement: Taking expectations in \eref{in1} and using proposition 1, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0$ yields \be r_{m} = E(y_{m}(i)) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E(x_{m}(j)) = 0. \enum{in201} \ee Therefore, $u_{m}^{2} = Var(y_{m}(i)) = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right) - \left(E(y_{m}(i))\right)^{2} = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right)$. Using \eref{in1}, \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= E\left(\sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right)^{2} \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) + 2\sum E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right). \\ \enum{in203} \end{split} \ee From proposition 1, ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ and ${\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)$ will (a) be independent of each other, and (b) be independent of $x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)$. Using these results, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0 $ gives \newline \be E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right) = E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E({\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l))E(x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)) = 0. \enum{in2041} \ee \newline Plugging \eref{in2041} into \eref{in203} gives
nodes.statement_short: Take expectations in the recursion, use Proposition 1 to kill the cross terms, and sum the diagonal second moments.

nodes.name: Mean of the pre-activation is zero
nodes.statement: Taking expectations in \eref{in1} and using proposition 1, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0$ yields \be r_{m} = E(y_{m}(i)) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E(x_{m}(j)) = 0. \enum{in201} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 1 and $E(W)=0$ to get $r_{m}=0$.

nodes.name: Expand the second moment of the pre-activation
nodes.statement: Therefore, $u_{m}^{2} = Var(y_{m}(i)) = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right) - \left(E(y_{m}(i))\right)^{2} = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right)$. Using \eref{in1}, \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= E\left(\sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right)^{2} \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) + 2\sum E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right). \\ \enum{in203} \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Since the mean vanishes, expand $u_{m}^{2}=E(y_{m}^{2})$ into diagonal plus cross terms.

nodes.name: Cross terms vanish
nodes.statement: From proposition 1, ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ and ${\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)$ will (a) be independent of each other, and (b) be independent of $x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)$. Using these results, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0 $ gives \newline \be E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right) = E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E({\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l))E(x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)) = 0. \enum{in2041} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Use Proposition 1 and $E(W)=0$ to show every cross term is zero.

nodes.name: Zero mean of the pre-activation
nodes.statement: \be r_{m} = E(y_{m}(i)) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E(x_{m}(j)) = 0. \enum{in201} \ee
nodes.statement_short: The pre-activations have mean zero on the first pass.

nodes.name: Variance equals the second moment
nodes.statement: Therefore, $u_{m}^{2} = Var(y_{m}(i)) = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right) - \left(E(y_{m}(i))\right)^{2} = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right)$.

nodes.name: Second moment expansion into diagonal and cross terms
nodes.statement: \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= E\left(\sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right)^{2} \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) + 2\sum E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right). \\ \enum{in203} \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Expand $E((\sum_j W x)^{2})$ as diagonal second moments plus twice the cross terms.

nodes.name: Vanishing cross term
nodes.statement: \be E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right) = E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E({\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l))E(x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)) = 0. \enum{in2041} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Independence and $E(W)=0$ make each cross term vanish.

nodes.name: Variance recursion for the pre-activations
nodes.statement: \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= Nv^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ \enum{in204} \end{split} \ee for all $i$.
nodes.statement_short: The pre-activation variance is $u_{m}^{2}=Nv^{2}(s_{m}^{2}+\mu_{m}^{2})$, whatever the input covariance structure.
assumptions: The weights ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ are assumed to be independent identically distributed normal random variables with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$

nodes.name: Independence from the input covariance structure
nodes.statement: Interestingly, this result holds for any arbitrary covariance structure of the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer.

nodes.name: Large number of hidden nodes $N$
nodes.statement: To answer this question, I make the additional assumption that the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'; this assumption is reasonable given that most neural networks have several hundred nodes in the hidden layers.

nodes.name: Approximate normality of the pre-activations
nodes.statement: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.
assumptions: the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'
conclusions: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$

nodes.name: Proof of approximate normality of the pre-activations
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$. Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \be \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \ee where the last equality follows from \eref{in2041}. This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}. Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}). Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations.
nodes.statement_short: Show the summands $p_{ij}$ are mean-zero and pairwise uncorrelated, then invoke the Central Limit Theorem for large $N$.

nodes.name: Summands have zero mean
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Independence gives $E(p_{ij})=0$.

nodes.name: Summands are pairwise uncorrelated
nodes.statement: Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \be \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \ee where the last equality follows from \eref{in2041}.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})=0$ for $j\neq k$.

nodes.name: Summands are i.i.d.
nodes.statement: This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the $p_{ij}$ are independent and identically distributed.

nodes.name: Apply the Central Limit Theorem
nodes.statement: Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}. Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}).
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Central Limit Theorem, noting the conditions stay weak even without independence or identical distribution.

nodes.name: Conclude approximate normality
nodes.statement: Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $y_{m}(i)$ is approximately normal in most iterations.

nodes.name: Zero covariance of the summands
nodes.statement: \be \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: The summands $p_{ij}$ and $p_{ik}$ are uncorrelated for $j\neq k$.

nodes.name: Central Limit Theorem
nodes.statement: Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}.
nodes.statement_short: A sum of many i.i.d. summands converges to a normal distribution.
assumptions: $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables
conclusions: $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large

nodes.name: Derivation of the moments for activations differentiable at 0
nodes.statement: When $g(x)$ is differentiable at 0, we can perform a Taylor expansion in \eref{in2} about $E(y_{m}(i)) = 0$. Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored, \be x_{m+1}(i) \approx g(0) + (y_{m} - 0)g'(0). \enum{in205} \ee Taking the expectation in \eref{in205} gives \be \mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206} \ee This equation suggests that the expected value of the inputs to the $(m+1)^{th}$ layer has little dependence on the moments of the inputs to the ${m}^{th}$ layer. Using this result recursively suggests that for all layers (barring the first), \be \mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}. \ee Using \eref{in204} and \eref{in2061}, the variance of $x_{m+1}(i)$ can be computed from \eref{in205} as \be \begin{split} s_{m+1}^{2} = Var(x_{m+1}(i)) &\approx (g'(0))^{2} Var(y_{m}(i)) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + g(0)^{2}) . \enum{in207} \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Taylor-expand $g$ about 0, take expectations to get $\mu_{m+1}\approx g(0)$, then propagate the variance through the linearization.

nodes.name: Taylor expand the activation about 0
nodes.statement: When $g(x)$ is differentiable at 0, we can perform a Taylor expansion in \eref{in2} about $E(y_{m}(i)) = 0$. Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored, \be x_{m+1}(i) \approx g(0) + (y_{m} - 0)g'(0). \enum{in205} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Linearize $g$ about $E(y_{m}(i))=0$, dropping higher order terms.

nodes.name: Take the expectation of the linearization
nodes.statement: Taking the expectation in \eref{in205} gives \be \mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206} \ee
nodes.statement_short: The expectation of the linearization gives $\mu_{m+1}\approx g(0)$.

nodes.name: Recurse the mean over layers
nodes.statement: Using this result recursively suggests that for all layers (barring the first), \be \mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}. \ee
nodes.statement_short: Iterating gives $\mu_{j}=g(0)$ for every layer past the first.

nodes.name: Propagate the variance
nodes.statement: Using \eref{in204} and \eref{in2061}, the variance of $x_{m+1}(i)$ can be computed from \eref{in205} as \be \begin{split} s_{m+1}^{2} = Var(x_{m+1}(i)) &\approx (g'(0))^{2} Var(y_{m}(i)) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + g(0)^{2}) . \enum{in207} \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the variance recursion and $\mu_{m}=g(0)$ to get $s_{m+1}^{2}\approx N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2}+g(0)^{2})$.

nodes.name: Higher order Taylor terms are negligible
nodes.statement: Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored,

nodes.name: Linearized activation
nodes.statement: \be x_{m+1}(i) \approx g(0) + (y_{m} - 0)g'(0). \enum{in205} \ee

nodes.name: Mean of the layer inputs
nodes.statement: \be \mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206} \ee

nodes.name: The layer mean is nearly independent of the previous layer
nodes.statement: This equation suggests that the expected value of the inputs to the $(m+1)^{th}$ layer has little dependence on the moments of the inputs to the ${m}^{th}$ layer.

nodes.name: Mean of every layer past the first
nodes.statement: \be \mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}. \ee

nodes.name: Variance recursion for the layer inputs
General weight initialization strategy for activations differentiable at 0
nodes.statement: Using the condition $s_{m}^{2} \approx s_{m-1}^{2} ... = s_{1}^{2} = 1$ along with \eref{in2061} and \eref{in207} gives \be v^{2} = \frac{1}{N(g'(0))^{2}(1+g(0)^{2})}, \enum{in208} \ee
nodes.statement_short: For any activation differentiable at 0 the variance-preserving initialization is $v^{2}=1/[N(g'(0))^{2}(1+g(0)^{2})]$.

nodes.name: Generality of the initialization formula
nodes.statement: Equation \eref{in208} provide a general weight initialization strategy for any arbitrary differentiable activation function. I use the results developed in this section to analyze the optimal value of $v^{2}$ for two commonly used differentiable activation functions - the hyperbolic tangent and the sigmoid.

nodes.name: Backward pass constraints are unnecessary
nodes.statement: In their calculations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving} impose an additional set of constraints to ensure that the variance is maintained even during the backward pass. I believe that this is not required, since the requirement that the variance of the inputs at each layer be the same ensures that the gradient flows through in the backward pass.
nodes.statement_short: The extra backward-pass variance constraints imposed by Glorot-Bengio and He et al. are argued to be unnecessary.

nodes.name: hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement: For the hyperbolic tangent \be g(x) =\mbox{tanh}(x), \ee we have $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$.

nodes.name: Xavier initialization for the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement: Plugging these results in \eref{in208} yields \be v \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{tanh1} \ee which is precisely the {\it{Xavier Initialization}}.
nodes.statement_short: For tanh the general formula reduces to $v\approx1/\sqrt{N}$, i.e. the Xavier initialization.
conclusions: v \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}

nodes.name: Sequential saturation puzzle
nodes.statement: In their analysis of a neural network with the hyperbolic tangent activations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} find that the deeper layers in the neural network have a greater proportion of unsaturated nodes than the shallower layers. As is stated in their paper, `why this is happening remains to be understood'.
nodes.statement_short: Why deeper tanh layers have a greater proportion of unsaturated nodes than shallower ones was left unexplained.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Variance of the uniform initialization used by Glorot and Bengio
nodes.statement: To explain their finding, I begin by noting that in \cite{glorot2010understanding}, the authors initialize the weights using samples from a uniform distribution $\left(U[-1/\sqrt{N},1/\sqrt{N}]\right)$ having a variance of $1/3N$.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Variance contraction under the uniform initialization
nodes.statement: Therefore, from \eref{in2061} and \eref{in207}, with $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$, we have $\mu_{m} = 0$ and \be s_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{3}s_{m}^{2} < s_{m}^{2} \ee \enum{seq1} respectively.
nodes.statement_short: With weight variance $1/3N$ the layer variance contracts by a factor $1/3$ at every layer.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: $u_{m}^{2}$ decreases with depth
nodes.statement: From \eref{in204}, this implies that $u_{m+1}^{2}<u_{m}^{2}$ for all $m$ (i.e., $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$).
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Layer inputs are a tanh transform of a normal variable
nodes.statement: Furthermore from proposition 2, $y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. Therefore, $x_{m+1}(i)$ will be the tanh transformation of a normal random variable.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
conclusions: $x_{m+1}(i)$ will be the tanh transformation of a normal random variable

nodes.name: The tanh transformation
nodes.statement: Using results from \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{tanh}(y_{m}(i))$ will have a probability density function (pdf) given by \be f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1}, \ee where \be t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right). \ee
nodes.statement_short: The tanh of a $N(0,u_{m}^{2})$ variable has an explicit pdf in terms of $t_{y}=\frac{1}{2}\ln((1+y)/(1-y))$.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Plots of the tanh activation pdf
nodes.statement: Plots of this pdf for different values of $u_{m}$ (provided in Figure \ref{fig:tanh}) produce trends similar to those observed by the simulation studies of \cite{glorot2010understanding} (figure 4 in their paper). A comparison of Figure \ref{fig:tanh} and figure 4 of \cite{glorot2010understanding} suggests that $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, as is expected.
nodes.statement_short: Plotting the pdf for several $u_{m}$ reproduces the trends of Glorot and Bengio's figure 4.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Shape of the tanh activation distribution
nodes.statement: From the results in \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, we expect the activations to be (a) approximately normally distributed when $u_{m}$ is close to 0 and (b) bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1 when $u_{m}$ is close to 1.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
conclusions: approximately normally distributed when $u_{m}$ is close to 0
bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1 when $u_{m}$ is close to 1

nodes.name: Explanation of the sequential saturation
nodes.statement: Accordingly, since $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, we expect the activations from the shallower layers to be more saturated (i.e., more concentrated near -1 and +1), and the saturation in the activations to reduce as we go to the deeper layers in the network.
nodes.statement_short: Because $u_{m}^{2}$ shrinks with depth, shallow layers saturate more than deep ones, which explains the observed trend.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
conclusions: we expect the activations from the shallower layers to be more saturated (i.e., more concentrated near -1 and +1), and the saturation in the activations to reduce as we go to the deeper layers in the network

nodes.name: sigmoid activation
nodes.statement: For the sigmoid activation defined as \be g(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \mbox{e}^{-x}} \ee we have $g(0) = 0.5$, $g'(0) = 1/4$.

nodes.name: Initialization for the sigmoid activation
nodes.statement: Plugging these values in \eref{in208} yields \be v \approx \frac{3.6}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{relur} \ee
nodes.statement_short: For the sigmoid the general formula gives $v\approx3.6/\sqrt{N}$.
conclusions: v \approx \frac{3.6}{\sqrt{N}}

nodes.name: CIFAR 10 experiment with a 10 layer network
nodes.statement: To compare the initialization described in \eref{relur} with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}, I use a simple 10 layer neural network whose architecture is described in Figure \ref{fig:nnarch}. For my experiments, I use the CIFAR 10 dataset \cite{krizhevsky2009learning} comprising 60,000, $32 \times 32$ color images evenly split over 10 classes. The dataset comprises 50,000 training examples (which forms the training dataset in my analyses) and 10,000 test examples (which forms the validation dataset in my analyses).
nodes.statement_short: A 10 layer network on CIFAR 10 is used to compare the sigmoid initialization against Xavier.

nodes.name: Convergence comparison of the two initializations
nodes.statement: First, I train the neural network with the {\it{Xavier initialization}} for 10 iterations and compute the top 5 accuracy on the validation dataset for each iteration. Next, I repeat the process using the initialization stated in \eref{relur}. A comparison of the validation accuracies for the 2 cases is provided in Figure \ref{fig:conv}, which shows that the convergence appears to stall with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}, but proceeds rapidly with the initialization proposed in \eref{relur}.
nodes.statement_short: Over 10 training iterations Xavier stalls while the proposed sigmoid initialization converges rapidly.

nodes.name: Rectified Linear Unit (RELU)
nodes.statement: Instead of attempting to provide a general solution, I focus on the most important non-differentiable activation function used in the analysis of neural networks - the Rectified Linear Unit (RELU).

nodes.name: Derivation of the moments under the RELU activation
nodes.statement: Since the RELU activation is not differentiable at 0, the results from \erefs{in205}{in207} cannot be used to compute the optimal value of $v^{2}$. To proceed, I use proposition 2 and \eref{in201} which state that for the first iteration, $ y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. We are interested in in the mean and variance of $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{max}(0,y_{m}(i))$. The mean will be given by \be \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1} \ee Similarly, \be E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2} \ee Using \eref{relu1} and \eref{relu2}, \be s_{m+1}^{2} = E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) - \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2} - \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2\pi} \approx 0.34u_{m}^{2}. \enum{relu3} \ee For the variance to be maintained at each iteration, we require $s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 1$ which yields \be u_{m}^{2} \approx 3. \enum{relu301} \ee Plugging \eref{relu301} in \eref{relu1} yields $\mu_{m+1} \approx 0.7$. By the symmetry of the problem during the first iteration, we expect $\mu_{m+1} \approx \mu_{m} ... \approx \mu_{2} \approx 0.7$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the mean and second moment of $\max(0,y)$ for Gaussian $y$, then impose unit output variance to obtain $u_{m}^{2}\approx3$ and $\mu\approx0.7$.

nodes.name: Set up the Gaussian pre-activation and the RELU map
nodes.statement: Since the RELU activation is not differentiable at 0, the results from \erefs{in205}{in207} cannot be used to compute the optimal value of $v^{2}$. To proceed, I use proposition 2 and \eref{in201} which state that for the first iteration, $ y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. We are interested in in the mean and variance of $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{max}(0,y_{m}(i))$.
nodes.statement_short: Use Proposition 2 to treat $y_{m}(i)$ as $N(0,u_{m}^{2})$ and study $x_{m+1}=\max(0,y_{m})$.

nodes.name: Compute the mean of the RELU output
nodes.statement: The mean will be given by \be \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Integrate to get $\mu_{m+1}=u_{m}/\sqrt{2\pi}$.

nodes.name: Compute the second moment of the RELU output
nodes.statement: Similarly, \be E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Integrate to get $E(x_{m+1}^{2})=u_{m}^{2}/2$.

nodes.name: Assemble the variance
nodes.statement: Using \eref{relu1} and \eref{relu2}, \be s_{m+1}^{2} = E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) - \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2} - \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2\pi} \approx 0.34u_{m}^{2}. \enum{relu3} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Subtract the squared mean to get $s_{m+1}^{2}\approx0.34u_{m}^{2}$.

nodes.name: Impose variance preservation
nodes.statement: For the variance to be maintained at each iteration, we require $s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 1$ which yields \be u_{m}^{2} \approx 3. \enum{relu301} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Require $s_{m+1}^{2}\approx1$, which forces $u_{m}^{2}\approx3$.

nodes.name: Recover the layer mean
nodes.statement: Plugging \eref{relu301} in \eref{relu1} yields $\mu_{m+1} \approx 0.7$. By the symmetry of the problem during the first iteration, we expect $\mu_{m+1} \approx \mu_{m} ... \approx \mu_{2} \approx 0.7$.
nodes.statement_short: Back-substitute to get $\mu_{m}\approx0.7$ for every layer.

nodes.name: RELU layer map
nodes.statement: We are interested in in the mean and variance of $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{max}(0,y_{m}(i))$.

nodes.name: Mean of the RELU output
nodes.statement: \be \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1} \ee
nodes.statement_short: $\mu_{m+1}=u_{m}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for a Gaussian pre-activation.

nodes.name: Second moment of the RELU output
nodes.statement: \be E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2} \ee
nodes.statement_short: $E(x_{m+1}^{2})=u_{m}^{2}/2$ for a Gaussian pre-activation.

nodes.name: Required pre-activation variance
nodes.statement: \be u_{m}^{2} \approx 3. \enum{relu301} \ee

nodes.name: He initialization for RELU activations
nodes.statement: Using this result in \eref{in204} yields \be 3 = Nv^{2}(1+ 0.49) \ee or \be v^{2}\approx 2/N, \ee which is consistent with that obtained by \cite{he2015delving}.
nodes.statement_short: The RELU analysis yields $v^{2}\approx2/N$, the He initialization.
conclusions: v^{2}\approx 2/N

nodes.name: 22 layer and 30 layer RELU networks
nodes.statement: In \cite{he2015delving} paper, the authors provide an example of a 22 layer neural network using RELU activations which converges with the {\it{Xavier Initialization}}, and a 30 layer neural network which does not converge with the same initializations and activation functions.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Pre-activation second moment under the Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: To understand why this happens, I compute the central moments of $x_{m+1}$ in terms of the central moments of $x_{m}$ when $v^{2} = 1/N$. From \eref{in204} we have \be u_{m}^{2} = s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}. \enum{r01} \ee
nodes.statement_short: With $v^{2}=1/N$ the pre-activation variance is $u_{m}^{2}=s_{m}^{2}+\mu_{m}^{2}$.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Mean recursion under the Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: Plugging results from \eref{r01} into \eref{relu1} yields the recursion \be \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{2\pi}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \approx 0.16(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{r02} \ee
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Variance recursion under the Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: Similarly, plugging results from \eref{r01} and \eref{r02} in \eref{relu3} yields \be s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 0.34(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{relu5} \ee
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Geometric decay of the moments under the Xavier initialization with RELU
nodes.statement: Simple manipulations of equations \erefs{r01}{relu5} gives \be \mu_{m}^{2} \approx 0.16 \times (0.51)^{m-1} \enum{relu603} \ee and \be s_{m}^{2} \approx 0.34 \times (0.51)^{m-1}. \enum{relu602} \ee for all $m \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Under Xavier with RELU both $\mu_{m}^{2}$ and $s_{m}^{2}$ decay geometrically like $(0.51)^{m-1}$.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Comparison with the cs231n simulation experiments
nodes.statement: These approximations are remarkably accurate, as is demonstrated by comparisons with the simulation experiments described in Figure \ref{fig:cs231ncomp}.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Why the Xavier initialization fails in deeper RELU networks
nodes.statement: Equation \eref{relu602} shows that the variance of the inputs to the deeper layers is exponentially smaller than the variance of the inputs to the shallower layer. Therefore, the deeper the neural network, the worse the performance of the {\it{Xavier Initialization}} will be. From \eref{relu602}, $s_{22}^{2} \approx 1.62 \times 10^{-7}$ and $s_{30}^{2} \approx 6.33 \times 10^{-10}$. Thus the variance in the input to the $30^{th}$ layer will be $(0.51)^{8} = 3 \times 10^{-3}$ times smaller than the variance to the $22^{nd}$ layer, and explains the possible reason why the 30 layer neural network described in \cite{he2015delving} converges, but the 22 layer neural network does not.
nodes.statement_short: The geometric variance decay starves the deep layers, which explains the differing convergence of the 22 and 30 layer networks.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.
conclusions: the deeper the neural network, the worse the performance of the {\it{Xavier Initialization}} will be

nodes.statement: It is surprising that the 22 layer neural network converges!

nodes.name: General analysis of non-differentiable activation functions
nodes.statement: Given the sharp increase in non-differentiable activation functions over the years, a more general version of my (largely incomplete) analysis of non-differentiable functions is warranted.
nodes.statement_short: A general treatment of non-differentiable activations remains to be done.

nodes.name: Role of non-linearities in the dynamics
nodes.statement: My analysis repeatedly illustrates the drastic difference in dynamics which can result from introducing non-linearities in the system.
